newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - July 8.

text.p: The daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. For further information on these articles or details of BMC's other international press and broadcast services call Simon McMillan on "44 (0)171 256 5130 or e-mail bmc.co@ft.com -- STRONG POUND HITS MANUFACTURING

The Office of National Statistics has revealed the strength of sterling in May caused the biggest monthly fall in engineering in over a decade and a 1.1 per cent fall in manufacturing output, its largest decrease in four years. London economists had predicted a small rise which led statisticians to halve estimates of factory output growth to one per cent per year. Simon Briscoe of Nikko Europe has predicted the Bank of England will raise interest rates, which will lead to an even stronger pound and 'further damage to the economy' revealing
'the shortcomings of the budget'.
-- UNION WARNS OF FURTHER BA CABIN CREW STRIKE

Union representatives of the 6,000 British Airways cabin crew staff set to begin their three day strike on Wednesday have declared that unless the airline negotiates a restructuring deal, it will call for a further three day strike beginning next Tuesday. The initial strike, which threatens to affect BA flights from London's Heathrow and Gatwick airports, could prove to be the worst industrial conflict in the UK civil aviation industry for years. BA has issued a statement to the effect that it would begin contingency plans to ensure as many flights as possible would operate on schedule.
-- TELECOMS GROUP TO OFFER FAXES ON INTERNET

US telecommunications group WorldCom International is to announce its entry into the $25bn international fax market by offering cut-price transmission via the Internet on Tuesday. WorldCom is the first venture to enter the Internet fax market and will launch the service from business centres such as London and New York beginning in August. The price of a fax transmission which would normally cost 30 US cents between New York and London could cost as little as six cents when sent over the Internet. US long-distance carrier MCI is believed to be currently planning a similar service.
-- FRANCE AND GERMANY CONFIRM EMU PLEDGE

At an EU finance ministers meeting in Brussels on Monday, German finance minister Theo Waigel and French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn reassured their Union counterparts they remained committed to meeting Maastricht criteria for Emu entry in 1999. Strauss-Kahn would not commit to the three per cent of budget criteria for 1997, but clarified France was prepared to take on extra austerity measures following a July 21st audit of public finances. Questioned on the three per cent issue yet again, Waigel asserted 'that means 3.0 per cent, do I have to be more precise', insisting his country remained committed to the target.
-- PROMOTERS SEEK TO GIVE POTATOES BROADER APPEAL

The British Potato Council has made a pledge to revitalise the 3.5 billion sterling potato market in the country for what it called 'Britain's buried treasure', by revealing plans to increase potato consumption by at least two per cent per year over the next three years. The Potato Council, set up to replace the deregulated Potato Marketing Board, stated it would no longer interfere in the market as its predecessor did, instead focusing on providing market information and improving industry competitiveness. TPC chairman David Walker identified a target market of '18 to 28 year-olds looking for adventure in their food'.
-- MINISTER UNAWARE OF EXCLUSION IN TV DEAL

It has been revealed that the UK government was not consulted over the Independent Television Commission's decision to remove BSkyB from the bidding for the country's digital terrestrial broadcasting licence. The National Heritage Department was aware of the ITC' position, but did not formally, or otherwise, approve the commission's action. National Heritage secretary Chris Smith is believed to have been pressuring the ITC of late to restructure the British Digital Broadcasting corporation (which had included BSkyB) and sources indicate Smith would have preferred BSkyB's participation as it would have ensured the successful implementation of digital television.
-- NTT EXCLUDES JAPAN'S TOP BROKERS FROM BOND ISSUE

Nippon Telephone and Telegraph, the dominant Japanese telecoms group has chosen to use Morgan Stanley and Merrill Lynch of the US to manage its forthcoming Y100bn euroyen bond issue in Europe. NTT announced the decision to choose US groups rather than any of the four Japanese securities companies was made for financial reasons as the US companies had made the best offers. The move is also seen as a further sign of intensifying competition in the Japanese financial markets in the run-up to the government's planned 'big bang' financial reforms.
-- WOOLWICH MEMBERS RECEIVE WINDFALLS AVERAGING 2,200 STG

Former building society Woolwich has abandoned its mutual status and floated on the Stock Exchange. 2.5m members have received windfall bonuses worth an average of just under 2,200 pounds stg, almost 80 per cent higher than January estimates. Shares in the group opened at 370p, but fell back slightly to close at 334p, and the flotation valued Woolwich at 5.34bn stg.
-- S ELECTRIC SHARE AWARD CRITICISED

Manifest, the proxy voting agency, has criticised the award of 21,062 shares to the former chief executive of Southern Electric made under a long-term incentive plan. The award was made just two months before Henry Casely stood down from the position, prompting concern from Manifest that there was nothing long-term nor incentivising about the awards. Casely made a profit of 172,860 when he exercised the awards last year.
-- ETHICAL ABANDONS FLOTATION AND CANCELS ACQUISITION

Cambridgeshire-based biotechnology company Ethical Holdings has cancelled the planned 14m acquisition of Irish pharmaceuticals group Clonmel Healthcare after abandoning its attempts to float on the Stock Exchange. Ethical blamed a lack of interest from investors, partly due to competition from other pharmaceuticals groups, such as Galen Healthcare and Powderject, coming to market. The failure of the Clonmel deal means Ethical will have to continue using contract manufacturers.
